title: A Kitchen for the Harbor
premise: August Voss, a wedding planner whose own engagement collapsed on the vineyard terrace he now runs, inherits his grandmother's harbor cottage and the letters she exchanged for ten years with a stranger she never met. The letters' author turns out to be Elias Marsh, the quiet fisherman who has just moved into the neighboring cottage, and neither expected to be reading their own hearts in someone else's handwriting. As August plans one last society wedding at the vineyard while the first harvest presses in, he must choose between the safe schedule he's built and a man who asks him to stay past the last train. He stays — the wedding ends, the grapes come in, and August and Elias begin writing their own letters, delivered by hand.
about_author: Dominic Vasquez spent seven years coordinating weddings along the northern coast before turning to fiction full-time, a career he describes as 'field research for heartbreak.' He writes from a converted boathouse and still cries at first dances.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: August's POV. He plans a flawless wedding for clients he envies and resents, then learns his grandmother has died and left him the harbor cottage. The emotional beat is numb competence cracking at the edges; he books a train he intends to take only one way, then back.

chapters.title: What the Will Left Out
chapters.summary: August's POV. At the cottage he finds dust, salt rot, and a locked tin box his grandmother's lawyer can't open. Flashback fragments of childhood summers. The beat is grief arriving sideways, through objects rather than memories.

chapters.title: The Neighbor with the Blue Boat
chapters.summary: August's POV. He meets Elias Marsh, who helps him when a storm tears the cottage shutters loose. Their ease unsettles August, who notices he's talking to a stranger more honestly than to anyone in years. Beat: reluctant warmth.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: August's POV. The tin opens: decades of letters between his grandmother and a correspondent signed only 'E.' August reads the first few, hungry and ashamed. Beat: the discovery that his grandmother had a secret inner life.

chapters.title: A Hand He Recognizes
chapters.summary: August's POV. Borrowing a pen at Elias's cottage, August sees handwriting identical to the letters. He says nothing, leaves abruptly. Beat: suspicion and a strange jealousy of a dead woman's intimacy with this man.

chapters.title: The Vineyard Calls
chapters.summary: August's POV. The Whitmore wedding — the largest of his career — demands his return to the vineyard, and its terrace is the same one where his own engagement ended. Beat: old failure resurfacing as professional pressure.

chapters.title: Elias
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. We learn his decade of letters to a woman he never met, how her words kept him anchored after his brother's drowning, and how he moved to the harbor hoping to finally knock on her door — a month too late. Beat: quiet devastation and hope transferred to August without his meaning it.

chapters.title: Second Draft
chapters.summary: August's POV. He confronts Elias about the letters. Elias admits everything except the one thing August most wants to know: whether the letters were love. August, furious at being a stand-in, retreats to the vineyard. Beat: rupture.

chapters.title: Centerpieces and Cover Stories
chapters.summary: August's POV. Wedding chaos: a bridezilla client, a collapsing florist, and August running on adrenaline and avoidance. He catches himself drafting a letter to Elias in his head. Beat: the mask of competence thinning.

chapters.title: The Letter He Never Sent
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias finds the final letter his grandmother-figure never mailed — she'd planned to meet him at the harbor the week she died. He brings it to August at the vineyard. Beat: grief shared for the first time, an almost-touch.

chapters.title: Rehearsal Dinner Rain
chapters.summary: August's POV. The rehearsal dinner, and the groom privately confesses he isn't sure. August, the man who talks couples off ledges, has no script. Beat: his belief system fracturing in public.

chapters.title: What August Believes
chapters.summary: August's POV. He tells the groom the truth about his own broken engagement on that terrace — the first time he's said it aloud. Beat: confession as self-liberation, even as it costs him professionally.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon, Half-Truths
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias comes to the vineyard during the harvest moon; they nearly kiss before August's ex, Daniel, appears as a wedding guest. August lets Elias leave without a word. Beat: cowardice and its immediate regret.

chapters.title: The Wedding Day
chapters.summary: August's POV. The Whitmore wedding unfolds beautifully — and August watches the bride's face and realizes she's as unsure as the groom. He must decide whether to stop the ceremony. Beat: the climax of his professional identity.

chapters.title: Speak Now
chapters.summary: August's POV. At the altar, August doesn't stop the wedding — instead he tells the couple the truth: that love isn't timing, it's choosing to stay. They wed, weeping, and August walks out changed. Beat: climax; his old creed dies.

chapters.title: The Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: August's POV. He drives to the harbor through the night, arriving as the last train pulls out. Elias is on the dock. August asks to stay — not for a weekend, for the harvest. Beat: the choice the whole book has turned on.

chapters.title: First Light, First Pick
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. The first day of harvest at the vineyard, August working the rows with Elias's hands over his. Beat: tenderness without performance; the beginning of something unscripted.

chapters.title: Reading Her Letters Aloud
chapters.summary: August's POV. They read the grandmother's letters together by the cottage fire, finishing the correspondence she left incomplete. Beat: mourning and gratitude braided together; her love legitimizes theirs.

chapters.title: The Letter August Writes
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. August writes his first-ever letter and leaves it in Elias's blue boat — an admission of fear, of wanting, of staying. Elias reads it at dawn. Beat: vulnerability rewarded.

chapters.title: What the Harbor Keeps
chapters.summary: August's POV. Daniel arrives to win August back; August declines without anger, finally certain. He signs a lease to keep the cottage and takes a local wedding — small, imperfect, joyful. Beat: identity rebuilt on his own terms.

chapters.title: The Reply
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Elias answers August's letter in person, reading it aloud on the dock, and asks the question the letters never dared. August says yes before he finishes. Beat: the emotional resolution, earned and unhurried.

chapters.title: A Kitchen for the Harbor
chapters.summary: August's POV, epilogue. One year later: the cottage kitchen rebuilt, the vineyard's second harvest coming in, a small wedding on the dock that August plans for free. He mails a letter to his grandmother's grave. Beat: inheritance reclaimed — memory as a place to live, not escape.
